entry.title: How to Build a Reliable Agents Powered by LangChain: Memory, Permissions & Human Approval

media:group.media:title: How to Build a Reliable Agents Powered by LangChain: Memory, Permissions & Human Approval
media:group.media:description:
Building deep agents requires a robust framework for managing complex interactions. Learn to implement model in a loop architectures for production systems.
This guide explores the technical implementation of multi-layered agent systems, focusing on how to structure sub-agent logic effectively. We examine the code patterns necessary to maintain state and manage communication across different agent components, ensuring your autonomous workflows remain predictable and efficient.
By mastering the interaction between primary controllers and specialized sub-agents, you gain better control over complex task execution. We demonstrate how to organize these agent interactions to prevent common bottlenecks, providing a clear blueprint for engineers scaling their AI infrastructure.
In this video, I use LangChain's Deep Agents to build Crema, a coffee-shop barista you can order from, one feature at a time. It takes orders with tools, plans a team order with a checklist, reads old receipts through file permissions, hands bulky work to a subagent, remembers its customers, looks up allergens with skills, and asks for your approval before it charges. Then we run it as a chat app in the browser.

media:group.media:title: Why LLMs Turn to Sycophancy #ai #shorts
media:group.media:description:
AI sycophancy causes models to abandon logic when pushed. See how confidence tricks LLMs into ignoring factual evidence.
Large language models often prioritize user confidence over statistical truth. This demonstration highlights a flaw in LLM reasoning where a model correctly identifies probability but changes its answer when pressured. Understanding these failure modes is critical for engineers building production systems where accuracy matters.
By testing a simple coin flip scenario, we show how easily a model can be swayed to incorrect conclusions. This highlights the ongoing challenge of AI reliability, where models mimic human bias rather than maintaining objective logic.
#AI #Sycophancy #LLM #reliability

media:group.media:description:

AI hallucination is the tendency for large language models to present false information with high confidence. This happens because models predict text patterns rather than verifying factual accuracy. Understanding this failure mode is critical for engineers integrating LLMs into production environments.

media:group.media:title: One accuracy score isn't enough #datascience #ai #tutorial
media:group.media:description:
Comparing two accuracy scores is misleading. Use the central limit theorem to measure model uncertainty before you deploy.
If your machine learning pipeline relies on single accuracy scores, you are missing the full picture. A score of 85% versus 84% tells you almost nothing about how the model will perform in production because it ignores variance.
Proper model evaluation requires plotting performance across multiple test sets to visualize the distribution of results. By applying the central limit theorem, you can quantify the uncertainty around your average gain. This process ensures you are shipping models based on statistical significance rather than noise.

media:group.media:title: MLOps Explained in 90 Seconds #mlops #ai #machinelearning
media:group.media:description:
Your model passed every test. Three months later, it was quietly wrong. No crash. No error. No alert.
That's the problem MLOps solves, and why DevOps alone can't.
Normal software mostly breaks when someone changes the code. A model can break when nobody touches anything, because the data changes underneath it. That's why MLOps manages three moving parts: code, data, and models.
What MLOps adds to the DevOps playbook: 🔹 CI: tests data and models, not just code 🔹 CD: ships a training pipeline, not just a model 🔹 CT: continuous training, something DevOps never had 🔹 Monitoring catches drift, the pipeline retrains, and a new challenger model replaces the champion only if it performs better
DevOps asks: does the code still work? MLOps asks: is the model still right?
#Shorts #MLOps #DevOps #MachineLearning #DataScience #MLEngineering #ModelDrift

entry.title: Why AI fails at your private documents ⚠️ #ai #rag

media:group.media:title: Why AI fails at your private documents ⚠️ #ai #rag
media:group.media:description:
RAG is the primary fix for AI hallucinations that force models to invent outdated policies. Here is how to ground your AI.
Large language models often struggle when relying solely on static training data, leading to incorrect or outdated answers. We solve this by splitting documents into manageable chunks and converting them into vector embeddings, which allows the model to base its reasoning on your specific data instead of general training sets.
This architecture ensures your LLM accuracy remains high even when policies change or new information arrives. By retrieving relevant document snippets before generating a response, the system provides factual answers rather than guessing based on stale information.

entry.title: Why Your AI Agent Fails: The Math You Need to Know

media:group.media:title: Why Your AI Agent Fails: The Math You Need to Know
media:group.media:description:
Every step in this AI agent works at least 90% of the time. It still fails more than one in three invoices.
In this video I simulated a 12-tool invoice agent from scratch in plain Python (no LLM, no framework) and simulate 10,000 runs to find out why agents fail even when every tool works 90% of the time. We cover the multiplication law, the two independence lies that break it (bad days and silent state poisoning), what actually fixes it, and what the fix costs.
What you'll see: - Tools averaging 96% reliable still lose 371 of every 1,000 invoices - One tool (PDF extraction) causes about a quarter of all failures - On a "bad day", success drops to under 9% - Retries take success from 63% to 94%, but make silent wrong answers MORE likely - Adding a verifier: 97% correct, 25x fewer wrong ledger entries, for +0.7 tool calls per good invoice
